newsitem.title: UK: Major hits Sinn Fein's Adams on soldier's death.
newsitem.headline: Major hits Sinn Fein's Adams on soldier's death.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major launched an emotional attack on Friday against Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's political wing, after the death of a British soldier in an IRA bomb blast in Northern Ireland.
"Don't tell me this has nothing to do with you. I don't believe you, Mr Adams, I don't believe you," Major said in his keynote speech to the annual Conservative Party conference.
"He (the soldier) was murdered in cold blood in the United Kingdom. I sent him there, Mr Adams, so spare me any crocodile tears."
Major's outburst marked a departure from his prepared text after he received news of the death of father-of-three James Bradwell in hospital on Friday.

Bradwell succumbed to 60 percent burns sustained in Monday's double car bombing of the British Army's headquarters in the province at Lisburn, 10 miles (16 km) from Belfast. The Irish Republican Army has admitted responsibility for the attack.
Adams maintains his political party, Sinn Fein, is not consulted by the guerrilla group on its campaign of violence designed to end British rule over the province.

"The IRA has always believed that Britain can be deflected by terrorism. They've always been wrong, and they're wrong now. No one will take Sinn Fein seriously ever again until they show a serious commitment to end violence for good," he added.
He praised Bradwell for having acted "in the best and most honourable traditions of the British Army".
Major's attack preceded a strong defence of his continued efforts to secure a lasting peace in the province which fears the IRA attack will lead to a resumption of sectarian violence.
"Progress has been slow, painfully slow, but progress has been made, and there is no other show in town," he said.
He appealed to the leaders of pro-British Protestant guerrillas to "stand firm". Loyalist guerrillas have kept to their two-year truce following the ending of a 17-month IRA ceasefire in February.
Major announced two initiatives designed to move the shaky peace process forward.
The British government will shortly introduce into parliament a bill aimed at encouraging people in the province to give up their arms by assuring them of amnesty from prosecution if they did so.

He also proposed parliament's Northern Ireland Grand Committee should get new powers, giving the province's 18 members of parliament greater opportunities to question ministers and to scrutinise government policies.
